scene_text_en: Once, by a wide river, a monkey lived in a jamun tree. Every day he shared his sweet jamuns with a crocodile who swam below.
The crocodile's wife tasted the jamuns and said: "If the fruit is this sweet, the monkey's heart must be sweeter. Bring it to me."
The crocodile invited the monkey for a ride. Midway he confessed. The monkey laughed: "My heart? I left it on the tree! Take me back and I will fetch it."
Safe on his branch, the monkey said: "Friend, hearts do not come off. But trust does." And the crocodile swam away, ashamed.
A hungry jackal crept into a town at night and fell into a dyer's vat of blue colour. He climbed out blue from nose to tail.
Back in the forest, no animal had seen a blue creature. "I am sent by the gods to be your king," said the jackal, and even the lions bowed.
One full-moon night the jackals howled. The blue king forgot himself and howled too. "A jackal!" cried the animals, and the king ran away.
A lion hunted so greedily that the animals made a deal: one animal would come to him each day, and he would leave the rest alone.
When the rabbit's turn came, she walked slowly and arrived late. "Another lion stopped me on the way," she said. "He says he is the real king."
Furious, the lion followed her to a well. He looked in, saw his own reflection, roared, and jumped at the "rival". The forest was free.
A crow, a mouse, a tortoise and a deer were friends. One day the deer did not come to the lake. The crow flew up and saw him caught in a hunter's net.
The mouse gnawed the net. The deer was free, but the slow tortoise had followed and now the hunter grabbed him instead.
The deer lay down as if dead; the crow sat on him pecking. The hunter dropped the tortoise and ran for the deer. The deer leapt up, and all four escaped together.
In a Buddhist Jataka tale, a great monkey king led his troop in a mango tree by the Ganga. One mango floated downstream to a human king, who tasted it and wanted the tree.
The king's soldiers surrounded the tree with arrows. The monkey king leapt across the river with a rope, tied it to a branch, and made a bridge of his own body.
Every monkey crossed over him to safety. Exhausted, he fell. The human king caught him and asked why. "A leader's life is for his people," said the monkey king.
In a Jataka tale, a king hunted deer every day, so two deer kings agreed to send one deer by turns and spare the rest.
When a mother deer's turn came, the golden Banyan Deer king went in her place and laid his head on the block.
The human king asked why. "She has a fawn," said the deer. The king put down his bow and promised never to hunt again.
A folk tale: a farmer bought a well from a rich man. When he came to draw water, the rich man said: "I sold you the well, not the water in it!"
The farmer went to Emperor Akbar's court. Birbal listened, then said to the rich man: "Fine. The water is yours. Then remove it from the farmer's well today, or pay him rent for keeping it there."
The rich man had no answer. He gave up his claim, and the whole court laughed.
Akbar drew a line on the floor. "Make this line shorter without touching it," he told his courtiers. They stared.
Birbal picked up the chalk and drew a longer line beside it. "There," he said. "Now yours is the shorter one."
King Krishnadevaraya gave every courtier a kitten and a cow, ordering them to raise fat cats. Tenali Raman's cat stayed thin.
"Why?" asked the king. "She will not touch milk, Your Majesty." The king did not believe him. Tenali put a bowl of milk before the cat, and she ran away hissing.
Tenali had once given her hot milk; she never trusted a bowl again. "The milk," he said, "fed my family instead." The king laughed and let it be.
One night Tenali heard thieves whispering in his garden. He said loudly to his wife: "Thieves are about. Let us hide our gold in the well!"
He dropped a heavy box into the well with a splash. The thieves waited, then spent all night drawing water to empty the well.
At dawn the box came up: full of stones. The whole garden was watered. "Thank you for your help," called Tenali from the window, and the thieves fled.
From the Hitopadesha: an old tiger stood by a muddy pond holding a golden bangle. "Take this gift, traveller," he called to a passing man.
"I am old and harmless now," said the tiger. "I only want to give." The greedy traveller stepped into the pond to take it and sank in the mud.
"Do not worry, I will help you out," said the tiger, and he did, in his own way. Dadaji says: when a gift is too good, ask why it is being given.
When Mitthu first flew down from the mountains to the villa, he could only say one thing: "Say it again!" Chintu laughed and Buddy barked.
Dadaji was teaching Chintu the seven swaras. Chintu forgot "Dha". Mitthu tilted his head and sang: "Sa Re Ga Ma Pa DHA Ni Sa!"
"Mitthu remembers everything he hears," said Dadaji. "He will be our Echo. When you forget, he will say it again, and you will say it after him." And that is how Mitthu found his job.
